cards.text: Psalm 130 is a song of ascents, and it starts LOW: the writer cries out to the LORD from the depths. Friend, I KNOW the depths. I spent years at the bottom of a junk drawer under a takeout menu for a place that closed before I even got there.

cards.question: Down in the depths, the writer begs the LORD to hear his voice. What does he want the LORD's ears to be attentive to?

cards.text: Then he asks a question that stops me cold: "If You, O LORD, kept track of iniquities, then who, O Lord, could stand?" Friend, if that list existed, mine alone would need its OWN junk drawer.

cards.question: The writer is saying that if the LORD kept track of iniquities, plenty of people could still stand.

cards.text: Nobody could stand, friend. Not you, not me, not even the expired coupon from my old drawer that believed in itself SO hard.

cards.question: Nobody could stand if the LORD kept track of iniquities. But then the song turns. What does the writer say is with the LORD?
The writer says that with the LORD there is forgiveness, so that He may be ___.

cards.text: Now the cry turns into waiting: "I wait for the LORD; my soul does wait". Not my kind of waiting, friend, where I open the oven door every ninety seconds to check on the batch.

cards.question: While he waits for the LORD, the writer puts his hope in his own plans.

cards.text: Then he shows just HOW hard he's waiting. Picture the watchmen up all night in the dark, waiting for one thing.

cards.question: The writer says his soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the ___.

cards.text: And he says that watchmen line TWICE. That's a man watching for the morning the way I watch an oven timer with nine seconds left.
Then he turns from his own soul to the whole nation: "O Israel, put your hope in the LORD". From the depths to calling a whole NATION to hope, friend, that's a comeback.

cards.question: The writer tells Israel to put their hope in the LORD. What reason does he give?

answers.text: Loving devotion and redemption are with Him
Their enemies have already been defeated
Their harvest will be bigger than ever

cards.question: The writer says the LORD will redeem Israel from some of their iniquity, but not all of it.

cards.text: Psalm 131 is another song of ascents, and this one is from David, king of Israel. He opens by telling the LORD what his heart is not.

cards.question: David tells the LORD that his heart is not ___ and his eyes are not haughty.
David tells the LORD that he goes after great things and matters too lofty for him.

cards.text: Then David says he has stilled and quieted his soul. Mine used to sound like the dead batteries I shared that drawer with, arguing ALL night over who had the most charge left.

cards.question: David gives a picture for his stilled and quieted soul. What is it like?

answers.text: A weaned child with his mother
A ship on a calm sea

cards.text: He comes back to that picture again: "like a weaned child is my soul within me." Friend, that's a soul that finally put the phone down and just sat.

cards.question: David ends by telling Israel to put their hope in the LORD. For how long?

cards.text: Notice that call: "O Israel, put your hope in the LORD" is the same line Psalm 130 used. One song starts in the depths, one starts with a quiet soul, and BOTH land right there, friend.

findings.problem: This story card only restates the answer to card 4 (nobody could stand) and still cites Psalm 130:3. It doesn't carry the baker to any new moment, so it works as a recap card.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage. No recap cards.

findings.problem: The blank asks the baker to finish the exact wording of Psalm 130:4 ("so that You may be ___"). No earlier card sets up the idea that forgiveness leads to the LORD being feared, so the baker can only guess the line's next word. The wrong answer "forgotten" also reads as silly next to "feared".

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The card says Psalm 131 "starts with a quiet soul." Psalm 131 actually opens with a heart that is not proud and eyes that are not haughty (131:1). The stilled and quieted soul comes in 131:2.

rule.text: Noticing: What he points out must be true.

findings.problem: The card cites only Psalm 131:3. It also points back to Psalm 130:7 ("the same line Psalm 130 used"). A single range covering both, Psalm 130:7-131:3, would include verses the card doesn't use. The output format only allows one range.
findings.question: When a story card points back to an earlier verse in the same passage that doesn't sit next to the verse it tells, what should its "verses" field cite: just the current verse, a wide range, or a list of separate references?
